options.metric: Annual number of motorists killed in police-reported NYC crashes
options.reason: An annual fatality count directly describes the observed number of motorist deaths, although it does not adjust for exposure to driving.
options.answer: Per-mile risk cannot be determined because miles driven are absent from the data. The annual motorist-death count fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 (26.4% lower), which is a count trend rather than an exposure-adjusted risk trend.

options.metric: Annual number of crashes with at least one motorist killed
options.reason: Counting fatal crashes measures how often a reported crash involved a motorist death without conflating multiple deaths in one crash.
options.answer: Per-mile risk cannot be determined because miles driven are absent from the data. Crashes involving a motorist death declined from 102 in 2013 to 75 in 2025 (26.5% lower), but these crash counts do not measure risk per mile.

options.metric: Motorist deaths as a percentage of all persons killed in NYC crashes
options.denominator: All persons killed in police-reported NYC crashes in the same year
options.reason: This composition measure shows whether motorists made up a changing share of all traffic fatalities, independent of the total number of deaths.
options.answer: Per-mile risk cannot be determined because miles driven are absent from the data. Motorists accounted for 37.0% of all traffic deaths in 2013 and 35.4% in 2025, about 1.7 percentage points lower based on unrounded values; this is a change in share, not a per-mile risk estimate.

answer:
The data cannot determine whether motorist death risk per mile declined, because it has no mileage measure; the annual count of motorists killed fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025.
The data cannot determine per-mile risk; crashes with at least one motorist killed fell from 102 in 2013 to 75 in 2025.
The data cannot determine per-mile risk; motorists’ share of all traffic deaths decreased from 37.0% in 2013 to 35.4% in 2025.
